subtitle: Pingala and the Secret Counting of Verse

panels.shot: dramatic three-quarter view of a scholar in dim lamplight, palm-leaf manuscript before him, patterns of syllable marks floating like an abstract grid around
panels.action: Pingala sits cross-legged beside an oil lamp, focused on a palm-leaf manuscript marked with sequences of long and short syllables, as ghostly rows of metrical patterns rise around him like a silent, ordered storm.

dialogue.text: In an age of chanting and verse, Pingala asks a strange question: how many ways can sound itself be arranged—and finds, hidden in poetry, a path that looks like binary.

i18n.hi: मंत्रों और कविता के दौर में पिंगल पूछता है: ध्वनि को कितने तरीकों से सजाया जा सकता है? और छंदों में छिपा एक रास्ता पाता है जो बाइनरी जैसा दिखता है।

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of an early Sanskrit learning center under open sky, students chanting in a courtyard, elders listening
panels.action: Under a clear sky, rows of young students sit in a courtyard, chanting Vedic hymns in unison while older teachers listen, surrounded by simple halls and trees.

dialogue.text: Centuries before paper and presses, knowledge moves by breath and memory. Verses are sung, not written; the shape of sound itself becomes sacred work.

i18n.hi: काग़ज़ और छापाख़ाने से सदियों पहले, ज्ञान सांस और स्मृति से चलता है। श्लोक लिखे नहीं जाते, गाए जाते हैं; ध्वनि का रूप खुद एक पूजा का काम बन जाता है।

panels.shot: medium shot of Pingala among other scholars, turning away from a group recitation to jot marks on a leaf, thoughtful expression
panels.action: Amid the chanting circle, Pingala sits slightly apart, head tilted, palms resting on a leaf as he carefully scratches tiny marks with a stylus, eyes following the pattern of the recited syllables.

dialogue.text: Most care about meaning and ritual. Pingala watches something else—the falling pattern of heavy and light syllables, the hidden rhythm that holds the chant together.

i18n.hi: ज़्यादातर लोग अर्थ और कर्मकांड पर ध्यान देते हैं। पिंगल कुछ और देखता है—गुरु और लघु अक्षरों का गिरता पैटर्न, वह छुपी लय जो मंत्र को जोड़े रखती है।

panels.shot: close-up on Pingala’s hand and manuscript, with long and short syllables marked differently in neat sequences
panels.action: A close view shows Pingala’s palm-leaf streaked with tidy rows: one symbol for a heavy syllable, another for a light, forming compact patterns across the surface.

dialogue.text: In Sanskrit prosody, each syllable has weight. Guru: long, heavy. Laghu: short, light. Arranged in measures, they make metres, the fixed frames of verse.

i18n.hi: संस्कृत छंद में हर अक्षर का भार होता है। गुरु: लंबा, भारी। लघु: छोटा, हल्का। इन्हें मात्रा में सजाकर छंद बनते हैं—कविता के तय ढाँचे।

panels.shot: overhead shot of Pingala surrounded by several leaves, each bearing different metrical patterns, his brow furrowed in concentration
panels.action: Seen from above, Pingala sits encircled by palm-leaves showing different sequences of heavy and light syllables, his brow knit as his finger moves from leaf to leaf.

dialogue.text: Poets know many metres by name. Pingala asks a harder thing: given a number of syllables, how many different patterns of heavy and light are possible at all?

i18n.hi: कवि कई छंदों के नाम जानते हैं। पिंगल कड़ा सवाल पूछता है: जितने अक्षर दिए हों, उतने में गुरु–लघु के कितने अलग-अलग पैटर्न बन सकते हैं?

panels.shot: slow push-in on Pingala’s intense face lit by lamp, background fading, suggesting an abstract problem taking over his mind
panels.action: Lamp light carves shadows on Pingala’s focused face as the world behind softens into darkness, leaving only his eyes and the faint scratching on the leaf.

dialogue.text: This seems a small puzzle of poetry. But to answer it, he must learn to list, without omission or repetition, every possible pattern. That means counting in a new way.

i18n.hi: ये कविता की एक छोटी सी पहेली लगती है। पर जवाब देने के लिए उसे हर संभव पैटर्न बिना छूटे, बिना दोहराए गिनना सीखना होगा। यानी एक नए तरह से गिनना।

panels.shot: medium shot of Pingala explaining to a young student, drawing a simple sequence of marks for 1, 2, 3-syllable patterns
panels.action: Pingala sits beside a younger student, calmly drawing patterns of one, two, and three syllables on a fresh leaf, while the student watches, curious and slightly puzzled.

dialogue.speaker: pingala
dialogue.text: If each place may be heavy or light, we must find a rule to reach them all.

i18n.hi: जब हर स्थान गुरु या लघु हो सकता है, तो हमें ऐसा नियम खोजना होगा जो सब तक पहुँच जाए।

panels.shot: diagrammatic over-shoulder shot of the leaf where patterns are built step by step from shorter to longer sequences
panels.action: From over Pingala’s shoulder, we see his stylus trace a column of two-syllable patterns beside a column of one-syllable patterns, then begin a third column with three-syllable combinations emerging.

dialogue.text: In the Chandahsastra, he sets procedures. Start with shorter patterns, then build longer ones from them, step by step, so no arrangement of heavy and light can be missed.

i18n.hi: छंदशास्त्र में वह तरीके तय करता है। छोटे पैटर्न से शुरू करो, फिर उन्हें जोड़कर धीरे-धीरे लंबे बनाओ, ताकि गुरु–लघु की कोई भी रचना छूट न जाए।

panels.shot: tight close-up on the leaf where a sequence of patterns resembles binary counting in columns of symbols
panels.action: A tight view of the leaf shows an ordered list: at each step a symbol flips from light to heavy or heavy to light, forming a ladder of patterns, column by column.

dialogue.text: Centuries later, scholars will notice: these rules match what we call binary enumeration. Each pattern mirrors a line where only two states—heavy, light—shift in fixed order.

i18n.hi: सदियों बाद विद्वान देखेंगे: ये नियम वही हैं जिन्हें हम बाइनरी गिनती कहते हैं। हर पैटर्न उस पंक्ति जैसा है जहाँ सिर्फ दो अवस्थाएँ—गुरु, लघु—तय क्रम में बदलती हैं।

panels.shot: medium shot of Pingala now marking a triangular arrangement of counts on another leaf, seeds of Meru-prastara
panels.action: Pingala begins to mark numbers on a fresh leaf, arranging them in a small triangle, his finger moving from row to row as if testing how they grow.

dialogue.text: To know how many metres use a given mix of heavy and light, he needs combinations. From his work grows Meru-prastara—a triangle of counts that later echoes Pascal's triangle.

i18n.hi: किस मिश्रण में कितने छंद बनते हैं, यह जानने के लिए उसे संयोजन चाहिए। इसी से उगता है मेरु-प्रस्तार—गिनतियों का एक त्रिकोण जो बाद में पास्कल त्रिकोण जैसा दिखता है।

panels.shot: wide shot inside a simple study room, shelves of leaves, Pingala carefully binding his Chandahsastra manuscript
panels.action: In a modest study lined with bundles of palm-leaves, Pingala kneels, tying a cord around a newly finished manuscript, the neat script of Chandahsastra visible on its top leaf.

dialogue.text: His Chandahsastra is not a book of electronics or machines. It is a short, dense treatise on metres—where his binary-like counting appears only as procedures serving poetry.

i18n.hi: उसका छंदशास्त्र यंत्रों या बिजली की किताब नहीं है। ये छंदों पर छोटा, घना ग्रंथ है—जहाँ बाइनरी जैसी गिनती सिर्फ कविता की सेवा में एक प्रक्रिया बनकर दिखती है।

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot of the same room fading into later centuries, showing changing styles of scholars and manuscripts
panels.action: The study room dissolves through time: figures in different dress come and go, manuscripts are recopied, the space slowly changing while the bound Chandahsastra remains at the center.

dialogue.text: Centuries pass. Prosodists quote him, recite his rules, adapt them. His name survives, but the hidden structure of his counting waits quietly for new eyes.

i18n.hi: सदियाँ बीतती हैं। छंदकार उसे उद्धृत करते, उसके नियम गाते, बदलते हैं। नाम बचा रहता है, पर उसकी गिनती की छुपी बनावट नए नज़र आने तक चुप रहती है।

panels.shot: medium shot of Halayudha in 10th-century attire, studying an older manuscript and annotating with commentary diagrams
panels.action: A later scholar, Halayudha, sits with an aged manuscript of Chandahsastra open before him, adding marginal diagrams and notes to his own fresh leaf beside it.

dialogue.text: Around the 10th century, Halayudha writes Mrta-sanjivani, a commentary. He draws out the structure of Pingala’s metrical enumeration, making its binary-like pattern more explicit.

i18n.hi: लगभग दसवीं सदी में हालायुध ‘मृतसंजिवनी’ टीका लिखता है। वह पिंगल की छंद-गिनती की रचना खोलकर दिखाता है, उसका बाइनरी जैसा पैटर्न और साफ़ कर देता है।

panels.shot: split-frame style showing a traditional Meru-prastara triangle on one side, a modern Pascal’s triangle on the other, echoing each other
panels.action: On one side of the frame a hand draws Meru-prastara, a triangle of numbers used for metres; on the other, a modern hand sketches Pascal’s triangle, the two shapes mirroring each other.

dialogue.text: This Meru-prastara, born from metrical needs, will later be recognized as the same combinatorial structure Europeans call Pascal's triangle—an independent discovery shaped by verse.

i18n.hi: ये मेरु-प्रस्तार, जो छंद की ज़रूरत से जन्मा, बाद में वही संयोजनात्मक ढाँचा माना जाएगा जिसे यूरोप में पास्कल त्रिकोण कहते हैं—कविता से निकली स्वतंत्र खोज।

panels.shot: modern wide shot of a university library reading room where a contemporary scholar studies printed editions of Pingala and commentary
panels.action: In a bright modern library, a scholar sits with printed editions of Pingala’s Chandahsastra and Halayudha’s commentary open, a notebook filled with binary numerals and Sanskrit terms.

dialogue.text: In our time, researchers like B. van Nooten and others carefully read these old verses and commentaries, showing how Pingala’s system corresponds to binary and combinatorics.

i18n.hi: आज के समय में बी. वान नूटन जैसे शोधकर्ता पुराने श्लोक और टीकाएँ ध्यान से पढ़ते हैं, दिखाते हैं कि पिंगल की प्रणाली बाइनरी और संयोजन-गणित से कैसे मेल खाती है।

panels.shot: close-up of the modern scholar’s notebook where Sanskrit metrical patterns are aligned with binary strings
panels.action: A close view shows the notebook page: each Sanskrit metrical pattern beside a neatly written binary string, with arrows indicating how prosodic rules map to binary enumeration.

dialogue.text: They do not claim he dreamed of computers. They show something subtler: in solving a poetic problem, he arrived at a way of counting that shares the logic of binary representation.

i18n.hi: वे नहीं कहते कि उसने कंप्यूटरों के सपने देखे थे। वे एक नाज़ुक बात दिखाते हैं: कविताई समस्या सुलझाते-सुलझाते वह ऐसी गिनती तक पहुँच गया जो बाइनरी के तर्क से मिलती है।

panels.shot: evocative low-angle shot blending Pingala in his ancient setting with faint overlays of modern mathematical symbols in the sky
panels.action: Pingala looks up from his manuscript in his ancient courtyard as abstract outlines of metrical grids and modern binary digits shimmer faintly in the sky above him.

dialogue.text: From chant to count, from verse to variation, his work reminds us: the desire to order sound can uncover deep patterns. Art and mathematics are not rivals; they are often the same search.

i18n.hi: मंत्र से माप तक, कविता से विविधता तक, उसका काम याद दिलाता है: ध्वनि को क्रम में रखने की चाह गहरे पैटर्न खोल सकती है। कला और गणित दुश्मन नहीं, अक्सर वही खोज हैं।

title_i18n.en: The Poem That Hid the Binary
title_i18n.hi: वो कविता जिसने बाइनरी को छिपा दिया

subtitle_i18n.en: Pingala and the Secret Counting of Verse
subtitle_i18n.hi: पिंगल और छुपा हुआ छंदों का हिसाब
